items.passage: Parvin took the window seat on the night bus through Tehran, as she had since they were girls, and Aigerim, her twin, let her. Between them on the bench lay the folded plan of their mother's house, each room already marked in two colors of ink. Aigerim had told no one that she had failed the licensing exam that afternoon, the one she had promised to pass before they sold anything. When Parvin asked whether she wanted the room with the garden door, Aigerim said it did not matter, and Parvin, without looking up, drew a line that gave her both that room and the study beside it. "You always liked the garden," Parvin said, as if the matter had been settled long ago. Outside, shuttered shops slid by under orange streetlights.

items.passage: When Siti walked along the seaside promenade in Hanoi each evening after working in Dewi's new garden, she carried the same black umbrella, furled tight, though the sky over the water was clear. Dewi, who had bought the house only that spring, asked once why she never opened it. Siti said it was for a storm that had not arrived. Their friend in the hospital on the hill had asked them both, that week, whether the doctors were hiding anything. Dewi wanted to tell her plainly. Siti only tightened the strap on the umbrella and said there was still time. On Thursday, rain came in sideways off the sea, and Siti stood under the awning of a noodle stall with the umbrella still closed, rain soaking her sleeves, until Dewi took it from her and opened it over them both. Below the railing, fishing boats knocked together in the swell.
items.question: In the text, the closed umbrella most likely represents
options: Siti's reluctance to face and share a painful truth even once it can't be avoided.
Siti's practical habit of preparing carefully for sudden changes in coastal weather.
the new house Dewi bought and the garden Siti tends there each working day.
Siti's wish to protect Dewi from the storms that often strike the promenade.

items.passage: Years later, Emre would still remember the cairn. When he came back from the army to the edge of the salt flat outside Cairo, he expected Hala to meet him with the cold silence she had promised in her last letter, the one that called him a deserter of the family. Instead she walked him past the drying pans to the low pile of stones he had begun as a boy, now taller than her waist. "One for every week you were gone," she said, setting another on top. He counted without meaning to; there were no gaps. That evening she showed him the ledgers she had kept for their father's salt works, every column balanced, a line left blank beside each month for his signature. Wind moved across the flat, lifting a thin white dust that settled on their shoes.
items.question: In the text, the cairn most likely represents
options: the resentment Hala had built up toward Emre during the weeks he was gone
Hala's steady, unbroken faithfulness to her brother throughout his absence
the family salt works that Emre hoped one day to take over from their father
Emre's boyhood ambition to build something lasting out on the salt flat

items.passage: Tell your mother you were with me the whole time, Weiqi said, pinning a wet shirt to the rooftop line above the Taipei alley. Zihan, who had wandered off the trail above the city for six hours before the ranger found her, watched the shirts snap in the wind. She knew the story was false; Weiqi had found her alone, mud to the knees, far from any marked path. But Weiqi said the truth would only get Zihan's hiking permit revoked and his own patrol questioned. Zihan agreed, and the lie settled between them like a stone in a shoe, small and impossible to forget with every step. All that evening she caught herself rehearsing it, changing a detail, then changing it back. Across the alley, a neighbor's radio played an old ballad over the rattle of an air conditioner.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like a stone in a shoe” most nearly suggests that the lie is
options: a minor but constant discomfort that Zihan cannot stop noticing
a heavy burden that keeps Zihan from walking the trails again
a secret that Zihan has nearly forgotten by the end of the evening
a protective weight that steadies Zihan against her mother's anger

items.passage: Did anyone else see the case fall? Layla asked the depot clerk in Beirut, though she already knew the answer. Her violin had slipped from the overhead rack when the bus braked, and Sigrid, her teacher, insisted that Layla had left the case unlatched. Layla remembered fastening both clasps. The driver said a passenger had bumped it; a woman by the window said no one had touched it at all. Each account was confident, and each was different, so that the truth seemed to splinter into pieces too small to hold. Sigrid examined the cracked bridge with her usual severity, then said only that bridges could be replaced and that Layla would practice on the spare instrument until Friday. Outside, buses idled in their bays, exhaust drifting over the ticket windows.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “splinter into pieces too small to hold” most nearly suggests that
options: the violin was so badly damaged that it could never be repaired
the conflicting accounts broke the event into fragments no one could join
Layla was too upset to recall what she had done with the case's clasps
the witnesses were careless people whose statements deserved no attention

items.passage:
Pass me the list, Marta said, and I did,
my mother's pencil hovering over names
while snow sealed the cabin door outside Samarkand.
Aydin's family, she wrote, then paused,
the letter I never sent her folded in my coat
like a coal I kept from going out
and kept from touching.
We counted chairs. We argued over lamb.
She did not ask, and I did not offer,
though twice her hand found my sleeve.
By the stove the kettle ticked as it cooled,
and the window held a square of blue dusk.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like a coal I kept from going out” most nearly suggests that the speaker
options: wishes she could finally forget a painful memory from the past
intends to raise an old grudge with her mother at the wedding
keeps an apology alive while not yet being ready to deliver it
plans to present the letter to her mother after the ceremony

items.passage: Chess rivals make poor confidants. I learned this at four in the morning in my aunt's bakery in Albuquerque, where Dainius and I had met to argue, as usual, though not about openings. My younger brother had asked each of us, separately, whether he should quit the club after losing every game of the season. Dainius wanted to tell him the truth: that he played too fast. I wanted to tell him he would improve. Between the cooling racks we circled the question like two kings in an endgame, each step careful, neither willing to come close enough to be checked. By the time the first tray of conchas came out, we had agreed on nothing except that my brother deserved one answer, not two. Kaya, my aunt, unlocked the front door and flipped the sign.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “circled the question like two kings in an endgame” most nearly suggests that the narrator and Dainius
options: played a slow game of chess while waiting for the bakery to open
competed fiercely to prove who understood the brother better
paced the bakery restlessly because they were tired and anxious
approached the problem warily, each avoiding an exposed position

items.passage: A folded bus ticket was all Solange ever left me. I had been her teacher for two years in the hills above Marseille, and in that time she had not said a word in class, though her essays ran long and fierce in pencil. On her last day before her family moved north, we waited together at the mountain bus stop, I with my briefcase, she with a backpack so full it seemed to lean on her. I had prepared a small speech about the proper way to say goodbye. I never gave it. When the bus came, she pressed the ticket into my hand, and on its back she had written a single line of thanks, the letters pressed so hard they had nearly torn through, a whole conversation squeezed into the width of a thumb. Genevieve, my colleague, later framed it for me. That spring, the broom on the hillside bloomed early and yellow.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a whole conversation squeezed into the width of a thumb” most nearly suggests that
options: the brief note carried all that Solange had never said aloud
Solange's handwriting was too small for the teacher to read
Solange regretted not having had more time to talk at the stop
the teacher squeezed in a hurried final lesson before the bus

items.passage: "Mend the heel, and I will pay you when we sing again," Stanislav said, setting one worn slipper on my counter. I am Dmitri; I fix shoes now in a stall near the old bridge in Tbilisi, but twenty years ago she and I shared a stage at the opera house, two sopranos who had sworn, she insists, to sing our duet together once more before we grew old. I remember the opera house, the dust of the footlights, the way she tapped her toe before every entrance. I do not remember the vow. I hammered the heel while she hummed the opening bars, slightly flat, and waited for me to join. My throat was full of leather dust and doubt. Still, when she reached the high phrase, I heard my own voice catch it, rusty but whole, and the man at the next stall put down his knife to listen.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The narrator recounts a past performance and then explains why she gave up singing for shoe repair.
A visitor invokes a shared pledge, the narrator doubts it, and she then acts as though it holds.
The narrator describes her stall at length and then contrasts it with a crowded opera house.
Two former singers argue over a vow, and one leaves the stall before it is resolved.

items.passage: When Rangi arrived at the hospital in Wailuku, his twin, Anahera, had already claimed the chair nearest the nurses' desk, a clipboard of their father's forms on his knee. For an hour they spoke only of parking and vending machines. Then Anahera began listing the rooms of the house in Paia: the lanai, the workshop, the bedroom with the warped door. He had been dividing it in his head, Rangi realized, deciding who would sell and who would stay on with the old man. Rangi had assumed the answer for years: the brother who never left would simply keep staying. But watching Anahera's thumb worry the edge of the clipboard, he saw how tired that brother was. So when the nurse called their name, it was Rangi who stood first, and on the drive home he asked which room had the better light.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes the waiting room closely, then recalls a childhood memory that both brothers still share.
It presents an argument between the brothers, then shows a nurse settling their dispute.
It moves from small talk to a hidden question about the house, then to one brother's changed view.
It lists the rooms of a house, then explains why the brothers agree to sell the property.

items.passage: Years later, Kamala still told the story of the night train from Kochi to Kozhikode, when she found herself sharing a compartment with Tara, the neighbor whose kitchen backed onto her own. For a decade the two households had been painting a mural along their common wall, a river in turquoise and ochre, and for two years it had stopped at a half-finished heron. Neither woman had said why. In the swaying dark, Tara admitted she had run out of the blue she liked and was ashamed to ask for money. Kamala laughed so loudly that the ticket collector peered in. She had stopped, she confessed, because she believed Tara had grown tired of her. By the time the coconut palms turned gray with dawn, they had sketched the heron's other wing on the back of a ticket.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A description of a long journey is followed by an account of the scenery at sunrise.
A disagreement between neighbors is introduced and then settled with a passing stranger's help.
A mural's history is traced from its beginning to the day it was finally completed.
A stalled shared project is introduced, and then each woman's hidden reason is revealed.

items.passage: Anh does not talk at breakfast. I learned this my first morning in the farmhouse his family rents outside Hanoi, where I had come as a guest of his sister. Tamar, his friend since childhood, sat across from him, and the two of them passed the fish sauce and the chili without a word. His mother apologized for them, calling them two stones. But I watched more closely. __When Tamar's cup ran low, Anh's hand was already on the teapot before she reached for it.__ Later, in the yard, Tamar knelt to retie a sandal strap that had come loose on Anh's foot, and he simply lifted his heel to help. Nobody else at the table seemed to notice. By noon the heat had pressed the rice fields into a single green sheet.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It gives an early sign that the friends' silence hides close attention, which a later scene confirms.
It suggests that Anh resents serving Tamar, a feeling that his mother tries hard to hide from the guest.
It shows that the narrator misreads the friends' habits, an error the yard scene later corrects.
It introduces a rivalry between the two friends that grows sharper as the morning goes on.

items.passage: What could a soldier at the city gate know of bread? Farhad wondered this as the customs man poked a rod through his sacks of flour, the same sacks Mehrnaz, his rival from across the bazaar, had sent back to him that morning with a mended seam. Last winter he had spread word that her ovens were cracked; her trade had never quite recovered. The seam was the work of a careful needle, small even stitches in red thread, her family's color. __He understood that a single sack, however finely sewn, could not undo what a whole season of rumor had done.__ The soldier waved him through. Farhad did not move at once. He turned the cart around, toward her shop rather than his own, while the mule complained and the gate lanterns swung in the wind.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals that Farhad believes Mehrnaz mended the sack in order to mock him in front of the bazaar.
It marks Farhad's sense that her gesture cannot match his harm, setting up his turn.
It explains why the soldier distrusts Farhad's flour and delays his passage.
It suggests that Farhad plans to repay Mehrnaz by spreading a new rumor.

items.passage: Canvas awnings snapped over Piper's souvenir stand on the Burlington promenade, where the lake wind smelled almost like the sea. Every afternoon Despina came to ask whether the postcards had changed. They had not. She bought one anyway, always the same lighthouse, and stood turning it over while she watched the ferry dock, waiting for word about her son's surgery in Boston. Piper, who had a dozen sharp ways to say that the rack was the rack, never used them. One might call the purchases foolish, and the gulls, at least, seemed to. But a woman who buys the same lighthouse eleven days running is not shopping; she is keeping a lamp lit, and Piper, to her credit, understood the difference. At four the ferry horn sounded, and the gulls rose all at once from the railing.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Despina's daily visits?
options: Amused contempt for a customer who keeps wasting money on identical cards.
Detached indifference that reports the visits without any judgment.
Impatient disapproval of a customer who distracts Piper from work.
Gentle sympathy that finds a hopeful ritual in a seemingly odd habit.

items.passage: Stale butter and dust hang in the lobby of the old theater on Central Avenue in February, when you are the only one buying a ticket. You came because Mr. Lior, your old chemistry teacher, wrote to say he runs the projector now. Twelve years ago you gave him a framed periodic table for his retirement, and he set it face down on his desk without a word; you took it as an insult and stopped writing. Tonight he shows you the frame hanging in the booth, its glass cracked and taped from behind. He had been ashamed, he says, that a pupil could afford such a gift when he could not afford to stay. You notice how carefully he has kept it dusted. You were nineteen, Talon, you tell yourself, and quick to read silence as a verdict. Below the booth, the curtain parts on an empty house.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the younger self's reaction to Lior's gesture?
options: Rueful self-criticism for having mistaken a private shame for contempt.
Lingering resentment that Lior never explained his silence much sooner.
Proud satisfaction that the gift has been carefully preserved for years.
Nostalgic delight in fond memories of the old chemistry classroom.

items.passage: Vienna's Westbahnhof cafe was where Konrad took me after the worst season of my apprenticeship, the autumn three of our staircases came back warped from a client's damp villa. I was twenty-two then, Camryn the American who measured twice and still cut wrong, and I expected a lecture. Instead he ordered two coffees and spent an hour describing his own first ruined commission, a cabinet that split in its first winter. I have since heard people praise mentors who never let you fail, and I find I distrust them a little. Konrad let me fail, then sat beside me among the departing travelers while it hurt. He did not rebuild the staircases for me; he only made sure I knew I could rebuild them. Outside, a night train to Munich was announced in three languages.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Konrad's way of handling the failed season?
options: Mild embarrassment that Konrad shared such a personal story in public.
Grateful approval of a mentor who allowed failure and then offered company.
Quiet frustration that Konrad refused to repair the warped staircases himself.
Skeptical distance from the idea that a mentor should ever intervene.

items.passage: Wet iron and diesel rose from the river the morning Soren asked me to stop translating for him. I had interpreted for him for six years, at every meeting with Dutch buyers, and out of habit I still leaned toward his ear whenever anyone spoke. We were crossing the old stone bridge to the harbor office in Rotterdam when he said, in careful, slow Dutch, that he wanted to make his own mistakes now. I felt something close to grief, which embarrassed me. I, Marit, had built a version of myself around being needed in two languages at once. In the meeting I kept my hands folded and bit back three corrections. Looking back, I am fond of that woman and a little impatient with her: she mistook usefulness for closeness. A tugboat pushed a barge of gravel under the arch as we left.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward her past reaction to Soren's request?
options: Bitter regret that she ever agreed to stop interpreting for him.
Unqualified pride in how gracefully she accepted the sudden change.
Affectionate but critical understanding of her former dependence.
Lasting confusion about why Soren wanted to speak Dutch himself.

items.passage: Why must every book in the workshop be sewn by hand, even the cheap notebooks sold to tourists? Emiliano asked this every Saturday in the bindery in Oaxaca, and every Saturday his stepmother, Emil, said only that it was the rule. A glue gun sat unused on a shelf, a gift from a supplier. One afternoon a tourist returned a notebook she had bought years before, its spine still tight after a flood had soaked her suitcase. Emil said nothing, but she set it on the bench where Emiliano worked. That week he stopped asking and began counting stitches without being told. Outside, a vendor wheeled a cart of corn drinks past the open door, ringing a small brass bell.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A tourist returns a notebook to the workshop after many years of use.
A stepmother uses a supplier's gift to make the workshop more efficient.
Rules that are obeyed without explanation should always be questioned.
A teenager comes to accept a rule once he sees evidence of its value.

items.passage: Imani had kept the boarding-house kitchen in Addis Ababa for thirty years, and she did not expect her son's new bride to change its rules. On her first morning, Jomo offered to translate the Amharic menu board into English for the foreign lodgers. Imani agreed, then frowned when a guest ordered the gentle stew and complained that it burned his tongue. Jomo explained that the Amharic word meant patient, slow-cooked, not mild, and that she should have chosen better. That evening Imani handed her the chalk herself and stood beside her, naming each dish while Jomo searched for the truest English. Neither spoke of the morning. On the windowsill, a pot of rue leaned toward the last light.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A mother-in-law comes to trust a new bride who weighs words with care.
A foreign lodger complains about the spiciness of a stew he ordered.
A new bride takes over a kitchen against her mother-in-law's wishes.
Families grow closer when they share household duties with one another.
